body.heading: A small magnet, free to follow a big one
paragraphs: A compass needle is a sliver of magnetised metal balanced so it can turn almost without friction. Freed to rotate, it does what any magnet in a magnetic field does: it swings until it lies along the field. Earth's field, at most places, runs roughly north–south, so the needle settles pointing roughly north and south.

The end of the needle that seeks north is called its north pole. Since unlike poles attract, the magnetic pole sitting near Earth's geographic north must actually be of the opposite, south-seeking kind — a quirk of naming that physics students have grumbled about for centuries. The labels stuck anyway.

body.heading: Nearly north is not exactly north
paragraphs: The magnetic pole is not at the geographic North Pole, and it moves. It currently sits in the Arctic Ocean off northern Canada, hundreds of kilometres from the true pole, and it drifts by tens of kilometres a year. So a compass rarely points at true north: the local difference is called declination, and it varies from place to place and year to year.

Serious maps print the local declination so navigators can correct for it — in some places the correction is a degree or two, in others more than twenty. Sailors, pilots and hikers who ignore it can be led steadily astray by an instrument that is working perfectly.

body.heading: An old invention that never retired
paragraphs: Chinese navigators were using lodestone compasses at sea by about a thousand years ago, and the instrument spread along trade routes to transform navigation everywhere: for the first time, sailors could hold a course under cloudy skies with no Sun or stars to steer by.

Your phone contains the compass's descendant — a tiny solid-state magnetometer that senses the same field. It is a humbling thought: the field generated by churning iron 3,000 kilometres below your feet is still, today, quietly telling billions of people which way they are facing.
